source.lemmas: Authored for EnglishAcademy in British English (US forms as notes), chosen by topic for CEFR C1. items.en: an idea that an argument is based on

items.en: a strong statement that something is true

items.en: a wrong idea based on faulty thinking

items.en: the reasons behind a decision or plan

items.en: a conclusion reached from evidence rather than stated facts

items.en: a claim that someone strongly believes is true

items.en: to prove that a statement is wrong

items.en: to reach a conclusion from evidence

items.en: seeming likely to be true

items.en: the process of using up so much of something that little is left

items.en: to damage the quality of land or water

items.en: to fill something up again after it has been used

items.en: to send out gas or light or heat

items.en: to reduce the CO2 released by an industry or country

items.en: a natural area such as a forest that absorbs more CO2 than it gives out

items.en: a layer of rock underground that holds water

items.en: the planting of trees in an area where they were cut down

items.en: liquid waste that a factory or sewage works sends into rivers

items.en: connected with living things and their surroundings

items.en: a person who works to protect nature from harm

items.en: a person who works to protect wild animals and natural places

items.en: (disapproving) false claims that a company is good for nature

items.en: not yet used though it could be

items.en: using heat from deep inside the Earth
items.example: Iceland produces much of its heating from geothermal energy.

items.en: producing power from the force of moving water
items.example: A huge hydroelectric dam supplies power to the valley.

items.en: so plentiful that it can never be used up
items.example: People once believed the ocean's fish supply was inexhaustible.

items.en: in its original perfect state and untouched by humans
items.example: The island's pristine beaches attract few visitors.

items.en: the work of cutting down trees for wood

items.en: an accident in which a ship leaks dark liquid fuel into the sea
items.example: The oil spill killed thousands of seabirds along the coast.

items.en: the careful looking after of land or resources for the future
items.example: Good stewardship of the land is essential for future generations.

items.en: falling water that contains chemicals from factory smoke and harms trees

items.en: the destruction of the natural places where animals and plants live
items.example: Habitat loss is the main reason many bird species are declining.

items.en: the screen or system a person uses to control a computer

items.en: a small fault that stops something working properly
items.example: A software glitch delayed hundreds of flights.

items.en: the ability of two systems to work together
items.example: Check the compatibility of the printer with your laptop.

items.en: a failure of a machine or system to work correctly
items.example: A software malfunction grounded the airline's flights for a day.

items.en: a period when power or a service stops working

items.en: a way to avoid a problem without actually solving it
items.example: Until the update arrives the IT team has found a simple workaround.

items.en: the short delay before a signal or information arrives

items.en: one version of something that is improved step by step
items.example: The latest iteration of the app is much faster.

items.en: the protection of computers and information from attack

items.en: a place where a computer stores information for quick access

items.en: the permanent program built into a piece of equipment
items.example: Update the firmware before you connect the router.

items.en: a screen that shows the most important information at a glance
items.example: The dashboard shows sales figures in real time.

items.en: to find and remove faults in a computer program

items.en: to find and fix the cause of a problem in a system
items.example: Technicians troubleshoot network faults around the clock.

items.en: to set up equipment or software so that it works as you want
items.example: Kwame configured the router to block unknown devices.

items.en: to change information into a form a computer can use
items.example: The library is digitising its oldest manuscripts.

items.en: to put new software or equipment into use
items.example: The team deploys updates every Friday.

items.en: to make a new product or system available gradually
items.example: The company will roll out the update next month.

items.en: to make devices or files show the same up-to-date information
items.example: The app synchronises your notes across all your devices.

items.en: able to grow to handle more users or work
items.example: We need a scalable system that can cope with rapid growth.

items.en: smooth and without any breaks or problems
items.example: The new app offers seamless payment between devices.

items.en: easy to understand and use without instructions
items.example: The software is intuitive even for first-time users.

items.en: with a code that anyone can see and change
items.example: The team built the tool on open-source software.

items.en: using the newest and most advanced methods or equipment
items.example: The hospital has a state-of-the-art computer system.

items.en: owned by one company and not free for others to use
items.example: The firm refuses to share its proprietary software.

items.en: a way of presenting facts to make something look better
items.example: The minister put a positive spin on the poor figures.

items.en: photographers who follow famous people to take pictures
items.example: The paparazzi waited outside the hotel all night.

items.en: all the people who buy or look at a newspaper
items.example: The magazine has lost a third of its readership.

items.en: a short news report on radio or television
items.example: The radio bulletin said that all the roads were closed.

items.en: a false story that is spread to damage someone's reputation
items.example: The councillor called the article a malicious smear.

items.en: the act of damaging a person's good name with false statements

items.en: an expert who is often asked for opinions in the media
items.example: Football pundits disagreed about who would win the league.

items.en: the act of telling something that was secret
items.example: The disclosure of the documents embarrassed the council.

items.en: a way of showing a story that favours one point of view
items.example: The article has a strong anti-business slant.

items.en: a short clip from a speech chosen for the news

items.en: (disapproving) a person or newspaper that speaks for a group
items.example: Critics say the paper is just a mouthpiece for big business.

items.en: a piece in a newspaper about a person who has just died
items.example: The newspaper printed a long obituary of the famous poet.

items.en: to find something that was hidden or secret
items.example: Reporters unearthed documents showing that the council knew about the danger.

items.en: (formal) to tell something that was secret
items.example: The lawyer refused to divulge the names of her clients.

items.en: (formal) to hide parts of a document before it is published

items.en: to make a story less shocking by removing unpleasant details
items.example: The broadcaster sanitised its report to avoid upsetting viewers.

items.en: to stop something from developing or being expressed

items.en: trying to find hidden facts by careful research
items.example: She won an award for investigative journalism.

items.en: (disapproving) showing too much interest in sex
items.example: The tabloid printed salacious details about the actor's private life.

items.en: likely to make people angry or violent
items.example: The editor was sacked after an inflammatory comment piece.

items.en: not shown to be real by any evidence
items.example: The paper printed unsubstantiated claims about the mayor.

items.en: given to only one newspaper or channel

items.en: (formal) spreading false and shocking stories about someone
items.example: The paper printed scurrilous rumours about the headteacher.

items.en: (informal) a long speech that is used to persuade people
items.example: The salesman gave us his usual spiel about the special offer.

items.en: something you suggest without saying it directly

items.en: the ability to say difficult things without upsetting people

items.en: the state of having more than one possible meaning

items.en: skill in making powerful speeches
items.example: Her oratory could silence a noisy hall within seconds.

items.en: the main idea of something without the details
items.example: I missed the start but I got the gist of the story.

items.en: a hidden feeling that you can hear in someone's voice

items.en: a hidden meaning below the words that are said

items.en: a long speech by one person

items.en: (formal) a quick sharp answer to a remark
items.example: His witty rejoinder made the whole room laugh.

items.en: a change in the sound of your voice as you speak

items.en: (formal) to strongly urge someone to do something
items.example: The coach exhorted the players to give everything.

items.en: speaking or writing clearly and with power

items.en: causing strong feelings in people
items.example: Animal testing is an emotive subject that divides families.

items.en: clear and simple to understand
items.example: His lucid explanation made a difficult theory seem simple.

items.en: honest and direct even when it is uncomfortable
items.example: In a candid interview she admitted that she had made mistakes.

items.en: completely clear and leaving no doubt
items.example: The answer was an unequivocal no.

items.en: saying what you think in an open and direct way
